chief_complaint: sudden right foot drop, slapping gait, inability to dorsiflex foot, and numbness over web space after prolonged squatting (Common Fibular / Peroneal Nerve Mononeuropathy)
hpi_details: 45M tile floor installer presents with sudden onset of weakness in his right foot discovered 3 days ago after working an 8-hour shift kneeling and squatting on hard concrete. Noticed his right foot was dragging when walking (`my toes catch on the carpet`) and he has to lift his right knee high with each step (`slapping/steppage gait`) to keep from tripping. Unable to lift his foot or toes upward. Also reports numbness and tingling on the top of his foot and between his big toe and second toe. Denies low back pain or radiating leg pain.
ideas: anxious because he cannot walk safely or perform his tile installation job without tripping
concerns: worried he suffered a stroke or slipped a spinal disc in his back
expectations: wants nerve testing, a brace to hold his foot up, and physical therapy to heal the nerve

clinical_knowledge.topic: Common Fibular Nerve Compression evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Common Fibular Nerve Compression is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes ankle-foot orthosis bracing, targeted physical therapy, and electrodiagnostic testing to localize the compression and guide prognosis, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden right foot drop, slapping gait, inability to dorsiflex foot, and numbness over web space after prolonged squatting (Common Fibular / Peroneal Nerve Mononeuropathy)

Key HPI features: 45M tile floor installer presents with sudden onset of weakness in his right foot discovered 3 days ago after working an 8-hour shift kneeling and squatting on hard concrete. Noticed his right foot was dragging when walking (`my toes catch on the carpet`) and he has to lift his right knee high with each step (`slapping/steppage gait`) to keep from tripping. Unable to lift his foot or toes upward. Also reports numbness and tingling on the top of his foot and between his big toe and second toe. Denies low back pain or radiating leg pain.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 72, BP 122/78. Neurological and musculoskeletal exam of right lower extremity reveals: 1. Motor strength: Ankle Dorsiflexion (Tibialis Anterior) is 1/5; Toe Extension (Extensor Hallucis Longus) is 1/5; Foot Eversion (Peroneus Longus/Brevis) is 2/5. CRITICAL DIFFERENTIAL CHECK: Ankle Inversion (Tibialis Posterior, innervated by the Tibial nerve from L4-L5 root) is completely NORMAL at 5/5, and Ankle Plantarflexion (Gastrocnemius) is 5/5. 2. Sensory: decreased sensation (hypoesthesia) over the anterolateral lower leg and the dorsal web space between the 1st and 2nd digits (Deep/Superficial Fibular nerve distribution). 3. Reflexes: Right patellar and Achilles reflexes are normal 2+ and symmetric. Tinel sign is positive with gentle percussion over the common fibular nerve wrapping around the lateral neck of the fibula.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Common Fibular Nerve Compression.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to L5 radiculopathy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Bowel or bladder dysfunction (cauda equina risk).
management_principles: Orthotic management: prescribe an off-the-shelf or custom molded, lightweight, carbon-fiber or plastic Ankle-Foot Orthosis (AFO - posterior leaf spring or solid ankle AFO) immediately to maintain ankle dorsiflexion during swing phase, prevent toe-dragging/falls, and correct the compensatory steppage gait while nerve regeneration occurs

Physical/Occupational Therapy: initiate targeted stretching of the Achilles tendon/gastrocnemius (to prevent secondary equinus contractures) and electrical stimulation/strengthening of the dorsiflexors

Electrodiagnostic testing: schedule Electromyography and Nerve Conduction Studies (EMG/NCS) at 3-4 weeks post-onset (allowing sufficient time for Wallerian degeneration to manifest clearly) to localize exact compression site across fibular head and determine prognostic axonal loss versus demyelinating neuropraxia
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 45M presenting with acute unilateral foot drop, high-stepping slapping gait, and dorsal foot paresthesias following prolonged compression at the fibular head, classic for Common Fibular (Peroneal) Nerve compression neuropathy.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 72, BP 122/78. Neurological and musculoskeletal exam of right lower extremity reveals: 1. Motor strength: Ankle Dorsiflexion (Tibialis Anterior) is 1/5; Toe Extension (Extensor Hallucis Longus) is 1/5; Foot Eversion (Peroneus Longus/Brevis) is 2/5. CRITICAL DIFFERENTIAL CHECK: Ankle Inversion (Tibialis Posterior, innervated by the Tibial nerve from L4-L5 root) is completely NORMAL at 5/5, and Ankle Plantarflexion (Gastrocnemius) is 5/5. 2. Sensory: decreased sensation (hypoesthesia) over the anterolateral lower leg and the dorsal web space between the 1st and 2nd digits (Deep/Superficial Fibular nerve distribution). 3. Reflexes: Right patellar and Achilles reflexes are normal 2+ and symmetric. Tinel sign is positive with gentle percussion over the common fibular nerve wrapping around the lateral neck of the fibula.
reference_soap.assessment: Right Common Fibular (Peroneal) Nerve Compression Mononeuropathy at the Fibular Head causing Acute Foot Drop.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Arrange prompt gait and fall-risk assessment; an appropriately fitted ankle-foot orthosis may reduce toe drag while recovery is monitored. 2. Refer for rehabilitation-led range-of-motion, gait, and strengthening work tailored to examination findings; avoid prolonged squatting, kneeling, or leg crossing. 3. Consider EMG/NCS after an appropriate interval if localization, severity, or recovery remains uncertain. Escalate urgently for rapidly progressive weakness, new bowel/bladder symptoms, or features suggesting a central or spinal cause.

learning_objectives: Differentiate peripheral Common Fibular (Peroneal) Nerve compression at the fibular head (weak dorsiflexion and foot eversion, but NORMAL ankle inversion via Tibialis Posterior and normal reflexes) from L5 Radiculopathy / Lumbar Disc Herniation (weak dorsiflexion, weak foot eversion, AND weak ankle inversion with low back pain and positive straight leg raise)
Identify the lateral neck of the fibula as the vulnerable anatomical bottleneck where the common fibular nerve is compressed by squatting, leg crossing, tight casts, or prolonged immobility
Prescribe appropriate Ankle-Foot Orthosis (AFO) biomechanical bracing to safely eliminate high-stepping compensatory steppage gait and prevent trip-and-fall injuries during axonal recovery
Understand the optimal timing window for diagnostic EMG/NCS testing (3 to 4 weeks post-injury) to accurately assess spontaneous axonal regeneration potentials and rule out denervation

teaching.one_liner: Peroneal nerve entrapment at the fibular neck leading to foot drop, slapping gait, and dorsal foot numbness.
red_flags: Bowel or bladder dysfunction (cauda equina risk)

must_ask.say: Do you catch your toes on the ground or slap your foot down when walking?
Do you feel numbness or tingling on the top of your foot or between your toes?
Do you frequently cross your legs at the knees or wear tight knee casts?
Can you turn your foot inward, or is that muscle weak too?
Do you have any lower lumbar pain radiating down your leg?

history.answer: My right foot suddenly became weak three days ago, and it slaps down when I walk because I can't lift my toes.
It is definitely both; my foot feels completely limp when I try to pull it up, and the top of my foot and toes feel numb and tingly.
The weakness is isolated to my right foot and toes, while the numbness is on the outer part of my lower right leg and the top of my foot, especially between the big toe and second toe.
It started abruptly three days ago in the morning after I finished an eight-hour shift of tiling on concrete; my foot was completely normal prior to that.
It has remained steady since it started three days ago, neither getting worse nor showing any signs of recovery.
My right toes keep dragging and catching on the carpet, so I have to lift my right knee unusually high with each step to avoid tripping and falling.
Nothing makes the weakness better, but prolonged sitting or squatting seems to aggravate the numbness and tingling.
No, I do not have any neck pain, low back pain, or pain shooting down my leg.
No, I have not had any facial droop, slurred speech, vision changes, or dizziness.
No, my bladder and bowel habits are completely normal, and I have no numbness around my groin or buttocks.
No, I have no shortness of breath, trouble chewing or swallowing, or drooping eyelids.
No, I haven't noticed any muscle twitches or thinning of the muscles in my legs.
No, I have had no fever, diarrhea, cold, or any other illness recently.
No, I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, heart irregularities, or a history of smoking.
I eat a regular diet with plenty of meat, I have never had stomach surgery, and I rarely drink alcohol.
No, I am not taking steroids, chemotherapy, water pills, or any other medications.
I am a floor tile installer, and right before this began I spent an entire eight-hour shift kneeling and squatting on hard concrete floors.
I do not habitually cross my legs while sitting, and I have not had any cast, splint, or tight wrap on my leg.
Yes, I can turn my right foot inward toward the middle without any problem; it's only lifting it up and turning it outward that feels weak.
I'm terrified that I might have suffered a stroke or slipped a disc in my lower back.
I am really worried that this might be permanent and that I won't be able to walk safely or continue working as a tile installer.
I hope to get nerve testing to find out what happened, a brace to keep my foot from dragging, and physical therapy to help the nerve recover.
I have always been healthy and have no chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I drink occasionally, perhaps one or two beers once or twice a month when socializing.
I work as an independent tile installation contractor and live with my wife in an apartment.
There is no history of nerve diseases, strokes, or muscle problems in my family; both of my parents are healthy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 99% on room air, and temperature is 36.8°C.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial movement, normal extraocular motions, and clear speech.

Right ankle dorsiflexion is 1/5, great toe extension is 1/5, and foot eversion is 2/5; right ankle inversion and plantarflexion are intact at 5/5, with normal 5/5 strength throughout all other muscle groups and no fasciculations or muscle wasting.
Decreased light touch and pinprick sensation over the right anterolateral lower leg and the first dorsal web space between the first and second toes, with normal sensation elsewhere.
Patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally; Babinski sign is absent with down-going toes bilaterally.
No midline lumbar spinal or paraspinal tenderness, and straight leg raise testing is negative bilaterally without radicular symptoms.
Percussion over the lateral neck of the right fibula elicits paresthesia radiating down into the dorsum of the foot (positive Tinel sign); calves are supple, non-tender, and symmetric.
Demonstrates a right-sided steppage gait with compensatory high knee lift and audible foot slap; unable to heel-walk on the right, but left heel walking and bilateral toe walking are intact.
